title: Trump Threatens to Bomb Oman Over Strait of Hormuz as Iran Standoff Drags On
excerpt: The U.S. president warned the Gulf ally it would face military action if it interfered with efforts to resolve the Iran conflict, escalating tensions in a nearly six-month war that has disrupted global energy markets.
body:
• President Trump threatened to "bomb the sh–t out of" Oman if the Gulf ally interferes with U.S. efforts to resolve the Iran conflict over the Strait of Hormuz
  • The war, now in its sixth month, has sent oil prices soaring and disrupted one-fifth of global energy supplies flowing through the strategic waterway
  • Iran insists on its right to manage maritime traffic through Hormuz, while Trump has demanded unconditional reopening with no tolls
  • Peace talks between Washington and Tehran remain stalled, with midterm elections looming in November

President Donald Trump threatened to bomb Oman — a longstanding American ally in the Gulf — if the country "gets in the way" of U.S. efforts to end the standoff with Iran over the Strait of Hormuz, according to Fox News reporter Trey Yingst.

"If Oman gets in the way, we'll bomb the sh–t out of them," Trump said during a phone interview on Monday, reported the Wall Street Journal. The president said U.S. forces could strike the Gulf nation if it interfered with the blockade of Iranian ships in the strait.

A Familiar Pattern of Threats

The latest comments follow a pattern of inflammatory rhetoric from Trump directed at both adversaries and allies involved in the Hormuz crisis. In late May, Trump told reporters during a cabinet meeting that Oman must "behave" or he would "blow them up," according to NDTV and AFP.

https://x.com/IranObserver0/status/2089313687701971180

"It's international waters, and Oman will behave just like everybody else, or we'll have to blow them up. They understand that, they'll be fine," Trump said at the time, according to The Business Standard.

The White House did not issue any correction or clarification after those remarks. The State Department later shared a clip and transcript without comment.

Oman, a key U.S. partner, has attempted to mediate the broader Middle East conflict and has itself faced attacks from Tehran. Iranian negotiators have held talks with Oman in recent weeks over a provisional arrangement to manage shipping through the strait, according to the Wall Street Journal.

A War With No Exit Strategy

The conflict between the United States and Iran, which began on February 28 when the U.S. and Israel attacked Iranian targets, has now dragged on for nearly six months. The Strait of Hormuz — through which about one-fifth of global oil supplies passed before the war — remains effectively shut.

"Hardly any ships are sailing through, at least with their transponders turned on," Bloomberg reported in early August. Most vessels using the strait travel on either a northern route close to Iran's shores with Iranian permission, or a southern route near Omani territory.

Iran insists it has the right to manage maritime traffic and has threatened to attack vessels that try to pass without permission. Tehran has also floated the idea of imposing tolls on ships and sharing revenue with Oman — a proposal Trump has flatly rejected.

"There's not going to be charging" for access to the strait, Trump said in early August, according to Bloomberg.

"I want to give them every last chance before decapitation. You'll find out today or tomorrow."

— President Donald Trump, speaking to reporters on August 4

Oil Markets and Economic Fallout

The prolonged disruption has sent energy prices swinging. Brent crude topped $100 per barrel in late July before falling back to around $85 in early August. The national average U.S. gasoline price has climbed to $4.10 per gallon, up more than 17 cents in a month, according to AAA.

The economic fallout extends well beyond the United States. India, which imports roughly 85 percent of its crude oil, is particularly vulnerable to sustained Hormuz disruptions. Higher energy costs feed directly into inflation, import bills, and household budgets across the Indian diaspora's home country.

For the estimated 4.5 million Indian-Americans and millions more NRIs in Gulf countries, the instability carries both economic and personal stakes — with family members, remittance flows, and business operations all exposed to the region's volatility.

What's Next

Trump posted on his Truth Social platform Monday that his "number one Goal" remained ensuring Iran "cannot have, in any way, shape, or form, a Nuclear Weapon." But he offered no timeline for ending the conflict, telling Fox News he was in "no hurry."

Peace talks between Washington and Tehran remain stalled. The Islamic Republic has vowed to retaliate fiercely against any major U.S.-Israeli strikes, and has demonstrated its ability to cause significant damage to Gulf states including Kuwait, Bahrain, Saudi Arabia, and the UAE, according to Bloomberg.

With November midterm elections approaching and polling showing 57 percent of Americans opposing the war, Trump faces mounting domestic pressure to find a resolution — even as his rhetoric continues to escalate.
image_caption: U.S. President Donald Trump has threatened military action against Oman over the Strait of Hormuz amid the ongoing standoff with Iran.
